papers.title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta's End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs
papers.abstract: Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators to reduce costs and mitigate vendor lock-in. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific optimizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. This paper presents our methods for optimizing alternative accelerators, using AMD Instinct MI350X versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X's 1.6x HBM capacity relative to B200). Second, our analytical performance model enables zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across diverse datatypes and matrix shapes in production models, drastically simplifying tuning. Third, increasingly mature agentic workflows have lowered the barrier to porting from the CUDA ecosystem; we extend these workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimizations and custom shim generation. Compared to the directly ported baseline, these methods deliver up to 1.5x improvement in end-to-end training throughput. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.

papers.title: Self-Guided LLM Reasoning for Error Diagnosis in Vehicle Routing Problems
papers.abstract: Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs) are fundamental to many real-world applications. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred progress in solving these NP-hard problems. However, most existing approaches assume that input instances are error-free, neglecting the presence of faults commonly encountered in real-world data. In this work, we systematically investigate the capability of LLMs to detect (and correct) errors in VRP instances, and identify key limitations, particularly in handling complex instances or errors that substantially increase the LLM's reasoning burden. To overcome these challenges, we propose a self-guided reasoning framework in which LLMs autonomously generate code that provides structured insights to aid in error diagnosis. Experiments across diverse problem settings and LLMs demonstrate that our framework significantly improves error detection performance, achieving near-perfect accuracy.

papers.title: Range: Decoupling KV-Cache Reuse Granularity from Storage Work
papers.abstract: LLM serving reuses cached key-value (KV) state to skip prefill, and growing contexts push that state past GPU HBM and CPU DRAM onto NVMe SSDs, placing prefix restore on the critical path of time-to-first-token (TTFT). We find that on a well-configured host-issued path the SSD is not the bottleneck: restoring the same 6 GiB of KV takes 2.1 s as 192 objects but 3.0 s as 6,144 objects, and more under layerwise loading, because every layer of the storage stack - lookup, allocation, I/O submission, GPU delivery, store, index - charges per logical object while the bytes stay the same. This cost grows with the KV footprint: longer contexts, deeper models under layerwise loading, and tensor parallelism each multiply the object count. Prior systems move this per-object work from the CPU to the GPU; the work remains per object. This paper presents Range, a KV-cache storage engine for vLLM and LMCache built on one principle: every cost on the storage path scales with bytes or physical batches, never with logical objects. Range tickets replace per-key lookup and ownership with token metadata and physical leases; byte stripes make the on-media layout independent of reuse granularity; completion-owned GPU transfer banks batch delivery and extraction and release each layer to attention as it lands. Range keeps the kernel cuFile path and changes four lines of vLLM. On a fixed 6 GiB restore, Range's median TTFT stays at 1.79-1.80 s across a 32x range of object counts and under layerwise delivery, within 70 ms of the prefix already being resident in GPU memory, while tuned in-process LMCache rises from 2.12 s to 3.01 s. Range improves on the fastest multiprocess DRAM-bounced path by 0.44 s at coarse granularity while moving no payload through host memory, and holds layerwise reuse at the cost of coarse-grained reuse, where the best stock path takes 2.24 s.

papers.title: CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion
papers.abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near-duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call \certex. Specifically, \certex\ stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that \certex\ returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, \certex\ is exact for every query at 7.1$\times$ to 18.0$\times$ the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact.

papers.title: Tree Edit Distance: Near-Linear-Time Approximate, Sublinear, and Dynamic
papers.abstract: Tree edit distance (TED), the analog of string edit distance (ED) for hierarchical data, is the minimum number of node insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one labeled rooted ordered tree into another. We narrow polynomial gaps between TED and ED in near-linear-time approximation, sublinear algorithms, and dynamic algorithms. We give an $n^{o(1)}$-approximation in $O(n)$ time and, for every $0<δ<1$, a $(\log n)^{O(1/δ)}$-approximation in $O(n^{1+δ})$ time. This improves the previous near-linear-time $O(\sqrt n)$-approximation [Boroujeni et al., STOC'19] and brings TED to parity with ED in this regime up to polylogarithmic factors. With query access to the balanced-parentheses (Euler-tour) representation of the input trees, we give the first sublinear-time TED algorithm: for every $τ\in[1,n]$, it computes a $τn^{o(1)}$-approximation of $1+\mathrm{ted}$ in $O(n/τ)$ time. For dynamic TED, we give an exact algorithm with amortized update time $\tilde{O}(k^7)$ and a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation with amortized update time $\tilde{O}_{\varepsilon}(k)$, where $k$ caps the distance that must be reported. The exact algorithm is the first to beat recomputation in a nontrivial parameter regime. The approximation improves prior dynamic guarantees [Das et al., FOCS'25] and cannot be significantly improved in any parameter regime without a breakthrough for static $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of ED. All results use dynamic programming on a new hierarchical tree decomposition, analogous to partitioning strings into blocks of geometrically decreasing sizes. It combines structural properties previously achieved only in isolation, providing a framework for transferring algorithmic ideas from ED to TED, with additional ingredients addressing the obstacles in each computational setting.

papers.title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

papers.title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling
papers.abstract: Generative visual verifiers play a crucial role in advancing multimodal intelligence. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique signal. Our experiments further demonstrate that these structured and interpretable outputs improve the verifier's generalization to out-of-domain multimodal critic tasks. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring at the global level. Under a general reinforcement learning framework, we first empirically demonstrate that the proposed pointwise graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in traditional text-to-image scenarios. We then extend our investigation to rule-governed generative world modeling where generative models are leveraged for world simulation and world reasoning under explicit rules. From a theoretical standpoint, we further show that a pairwise verification paradigm yields more accurate critiques than the pointwise formulation when ground-truth images are available, with empirical results on diverse structured world-modeling tasks such as Maze and Sudoku further validating the effectiveness of our approach. Overall, our findings suggest a key insight: the transition from generative models to structured world-modeling agents critically hinges on the availability of accurate pairwise graded visual verifiers.

papers.title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
papers.abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/
